newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA THE HERO BUT ALPHAND MORE LOCAL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-TOMBA THE HERO BUT ALPHAND MORE LOCAL.

text.p: It would seem a reasonable assumption to cast Alberto Tomba in the role of local hero at the Alpine skiing world championships which start next Monday.

The Italian triple Olympic and reigning double world champion won his first World Cup race on the Kandahar piste in 1987 and can count on the Tomba fan club turning out in force from nearby Turin and all over Italy.
But another ageing skier, far more successful on the circuit this season than the 30-year-old "Bomba" from the distant flatlands around Bologna, is also claiming the role.

Luc Alphand, once dubbed "Unlucky Luc" because of his recurring injury problems, may be French rather than Italian but he is one of few true local medal hopes in the two-week championships which start with a men's super-G.
Alphand was born in Serre-Chevalier, over the mountain and about 35 km from Sestriere, 31 years ago and has never really left the resort where he owns a small hotel.
He publicises his birthplace remorselessly.
"Sestriere is something different. The piste is beautiful and its almost like home -- there are the same sort of fir trees," the jovial Frenchman said recently.
After following up three downhill victories this season with a first career triumph in a super-G this week, Alphand will arrive in Sestriere as a gold medal favourite.
The World Cup overall leader, as well as heading the downhill and super-G standings, Alphand has never won a major medal in four world championships and two Olympics.
He was bronze medallist in downhill in the Sierra Nevada world championships last year.
He cannot count on the sort of following Tomba has -- no skier can -- but his fans will have no more than a short commute to the slopes compared to those of his rivals.
Italian Kristian Ghedina, also winner of three downhills this season, comes from Cortina d'Ampezzo near the border with Austria while double winner Fritz Strobl is Austrian.
Alphand will also be one of the first in action with the men's speed events scheduled for the first week.
Tomba, who usually stays well away until just before his events, has his first race -- a giant slalom -- on February 12 with the night slalom the last event on February 15.
The Italian has only completed a handful of races this season, with two second places, but has made Sestriere his main aim after almost quitting the sport last year.

"When in March 1996 I went to Lillehammer for the World Cup finals, after winning two golds in Sierra Nevada, I was determined to give up skiing," Tomba wrote in a signed letter to fans that appeared in the La Stampa newspaper last week.
"One of the reasons why I decided to wait, to think it over and eventually reject the idea, was that I would have had to give up the possibility of competing in Sestriere."

After injuring himself in training before the season started, and then suffering influenza after Christmas, Tomba has handed over the mantle of favourite among the Italian men to Ghedina but he remains the undeniable crowd favourite.
"Here the fans will arrive in force, we will feel all their affection," Tomba wrote. "Personally I need them."
He is right. In the slalom, Austrian Thomas Sykora has proved almost unbeatable this season while in the giant slalom the Swiss, Austrians and Norwegians have dominated.
Michael Von Gruenigen, double bronze medallist in Sierra Nevada, looks like Switzerland's best chance of a first men's gold medal in technical events for a decade.
The reigning giant World Cup champion, Von Gruenigen has won three giants while compatriot Steve Locher has also won one.
The Swiss won no gold medals at the last championships and only one in 1991 -- the men's downhill.
